context_blurb:
Hold your hands toward a campfire or grip a sun-baked railing, and you feel heat on the move. Heat is energy flowing from warmer things to cooler ones, and it travels in three ways: conduction, convection and radiation. Knowing which is which lets people trap heat or keep it out.

Left to itself, heat flows only from a warmer thing to a cooler one. It keeps flowing until the two things share one temperature, somewhere between where each began, and then the flow stops. Press a hot metal block against a cold one, with a thermometer in each, and the two readings move until they meet. The hot block is still warm then; what has gone is the difference in temperature that drove the flow.

Conduction is heat passing through matter by touch. In a metal rod with one end in a flame, the particles at the hot end jiggle faster and bump into their neighbours, passing energy along, while the metal itself stays put. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic and still air are poor ones. In the late 1700s many scientists pictured heat as an invisible fluid called caloric, until Count Rumford's cannon-boring work in 1798 and James Joule's later experiments showed it to be energy on the move. Conduction runs in every direction, down as well as up. The saying that heat rises is a mix-up: what rises is warm air. So an ice pack propped under a sore ankle draws heat down out of it just as readily as a pack laid on top.

In convection, the second way, a liquid or gas carries the heat as it moves. Warmed fluid expands, grows less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place; the loop is a convection current. To see one, let a few crystals of potassium permanganate, which turn water purple, settle near one side of a beaker, then gently warm the glass just under them. A purple streak climbs the heated side, drifts across the top, and sinks down the far side as it cools. Despite its name, a typical hot-water radiator gives off only about a quarter of its heat as radiation. Mostly it warms the air touching it, which rises and carries the heat round a chilly classroom in a convection current.

Radiation, the third way, needs no matter: it is energy carried by rays, mostly invisible infrared, which every warm thing gives off and which travel in straight lines, even across empty space from the Sun. Sit a few steps from a campfire and most of the warmth on your face arrives as these rays, spreading straight out from the flames in every direction. The fire's hot air rises straight up into the sky, and your back, in the shadow of your body, stays cold. A metal railing in bright sun is heated first by radiation, as the metal absorbs the sunlight, and then by conduction it passes that heat into any hand that grips it.

Insulators slow heat down. Still air is a poor conductor, but left free it carries heat by convection, so the best insulators trap air in spaces too small for it to flow. Fur, down feathers and fibreglass, a fluffy mat of fine glass threads laid in attics, all work this way. Solid glass passes heat about twenty times better than glass wool, so in a fibreglass mat the trapped air does most of the work.

In 1892, at the Royal Institution in London, the Scottish chemist James Dewar built a vacuum flask to keep his liquefied gases cold long enough to study them. Its glass is doubled, an inner bottle inside an outer one, and the air between them has been pumped away. Conduction needs particles to bump together and convection needs a fluid to flow, so the near-empty gap blocks conduction and convection alike. Radiation can still cross a vacuum, so the glass facing the gap is silvered like a mirror to reflect it back.

Shiny metal absorbs little radiation and reflects most of it. That is the secret of the space blanket, a thin plastic film with a shiny skin of aluminium, often wrapped round marathon runners after a race. Every warm body gives off infrared rays, and the aluminium reflects up to 97 percent of a runner's heat rays back toward him.
